title: Group 2
objectives: Describe and explain the trends in physical properties of the Group 2 elements Mg to Ba, including atomic radius and ionisation energy
Describe the reactions of the elements with oxygen, water and dilute acids, and the reactions of their oxides, hydroxides and carbonates with water and with dilute acids
Describe the thermal decomposition of the nitrates and carbonates, and the trend in their thermal stability
State the variation in the solubilities of the hydroxides and sulfates down the group
Describe and explain the use of Ca(OH)₂ and CaCO₃ (powdered limestone) in agriculture
Use these trends to predict the properties of unfamiliar Group 2 elements and compounds
why: Group 2 compounds are everywhere: limestone and lime in building and farming, magnesium hydroxide in indigestion remedies, barium sulfate in medical X-rays. The group is also the clearest example of how a trend in atomic size drives trends in chemistry, which is why it appears on every Paper 1 and regularly in Paper 2.
intro: The Group 2 elements all have two outer s electrons, which they lose to form M²⁺ ions. As the atoms get larger down the group, these electrons are lost more easily. This chapter looks at the reactions of the elements and their compounds and at the trends in solubility and thermal stability.

blocks.title: Group 2 trends
blocks.h: Switch between properties to see how each changes from Mg to Ba, with the reason and each metal’s reaction with water.

blocks.cap: Physical trends from Mg to Ba
head: property
trend
reason
rows: outer electrons further from the nucleus and more shielded; this outweighs the extra protons
the two outer electrons are lost more easily
larger ions, so weaker attraction to the delocalised electrons

items: With oxygen: 2M + O₂ → 2MO (white solids). Mg burns with a brilliant white flame.
With water: M + 2H₂O → M(OH)₂ + H₂, faster down the group. Mg reacts only very slowly with cold water, but burns in steam: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂.
With dilute HCl: M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂, faster down the group.
With dilute H₂SO₄: M + H₂SO₄ → MSO₄ + H₂. For Ca, Sr and Ba the reaction slows or stops as an insoluble sulfate coats the metal.
Oxides are basic: MO + H₂O → M(OH)₂ (no hydrogen). CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ is very exothermic ("slaking" lime).
Oxides and hydroxides neutralise acids: MO + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂O; M(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MCl₂ + 2H₂O.
Carbonates react with acids: MCO₃ + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Carbonates are insoluble in water.

blocks.wrong: Calcium oxide reacts with water to give hydrogen.
blocks.right: Only the metals give hydrogen with water. Oxides give the hydroxide only.

blocks.q: What forms when magnesium is heated in steam?
blocks.why: At steam temperature Mg(OH)₂ is not stable: MgO forms.

blocks.h: Consequences: a saturated Mg(OH)₂ solution has pH about 9–10 (milk of magnesia is a mild antacid); Ca(OH)₂ about 12; Ba(OH)₂ about 13–14. BaSO₄ is so insoluble that it is safe to swallow as a ‘barium meal’ for X-rays.

items: Sulfate test: add acidified BaCl₂ or Ba(NO₃)₂: a white precipitate of BaSO₄ that does not dissolve in acid.
A carbonate also gives a white precipitate with Ba²⁺, but it fizzes (CO₂) and dissolves in acid.
Adding NaOH to a Mg²⁺ solution gives a white precipitate of Mg(OH)₂, which does not dissolve in excess.

blocks.h: Remember the opposite trends: hydroxides up (more soluble down), sulfates down (less soluble down).

sections.title: Thermal decomposition of nitrates and carbonates

blocks.h: On heating a nitrate you see a brown gas (NO₂) and a gas that relights a glowing splint (O₂); the white solid may melt first. Hydrated nitrates give off water vapour first.

Thermal stability increases down the group: higher temperatures are needed to decompose BaCO₃ than MgCO₃. A small, doubly charged cation such as Mg²⁺ has a high charge density and polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the large carbonate or nitrate ion, weakening its bonds. Larger cations lower down polarise the anion less.

blocks.name: decomp
blocks.title: Thermal decomposition calculator
blocks.h: Choose a carbonate or nitrate and a mass. The calculator writes the equation and works out the amounts and volumes of gas and the mass of residue.

blocks.q: Calculate the total volume of gas (room conditions) produced when 3.70 g of anhydrous magnesium nitrate (M<sub>r</sub> 148.3) is heated to constant mass.
blocks.err: Counting only the NO₂ or using a 1 : 1 ratio for O₂.

blocks.h: Crops grow poorly in acidic soil. Farmers add a base to raise the pH:

items: Slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂: slightly soluble, so it acts quickly. Ca(OH)₂ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + 2H₂O.
Powdered limestone, CaCO₃: insoluble, so it acts slowly and lasts longer; harder to overdose. CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂.

blocks.q: Why is powdered limestone sometimes preferred to slaked lime?
blocks.a: It is cheaper and insoluble, so it does not make the soil too alkaline if too much is added; it neutralises acid gradually over a long time.

items: One mole of CaCO₃ neutralises the same amount of acid as one mole of Ca(OH)₂.
Ca(OH)₂ is less soluble than CaCO₃.
Ca(OH)₂ is slightly soluble; CaCO₃ is insoluble.

summary: Down Group 2: atomic radius increases; ionisation energies decrease; reactivity increases.
M + 2H₂O → M(OH)₂ + H₂ (faster down the group). Mg + steam → MgO + H₂.
Oxides are basic: MO + H₂O → M(OH)₂; MO + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂O.
Hydroxide solubility increases down the group; sulfate solubility decreases.
MCO₃ → MO + CO₂; 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂ (brown gas, glowing splint relights).
Thermal stability of carbonates and nitrates increases down the group: larger cations polarise the anion less.
Per mole of nitrate: 2.5 mol of gas (2 NO₂ + ½ O₂).
BaSO₄ is very insoluble: used in the sulfate test and in barium meals.
Ca(OH)₂ and powdered CaCO₃ neutralise acidic soil.

practice.q: Describe what you would see when calcium is added to water, and write the equation.
practice.a: Fizzing (bubbles of H₂), the calcium sinks/moves and disappears, the solution turns cloudy (slightly soluble Ca(OH)₂). Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂

practice.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy decreases from Mg to Ba.
practice.a: The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells; this outweighs the increase in nuclear charge, so it is removed more easily.

practice.q: Calculate the mass of CaO formed when 25.0 g of CaCO₃ is heated to constant mass.
Predict, with reasons, two properties of radium hydroxide and radium sulfate.
practice.a: Ra(OH)₂: the most soluble Group 2 hydroxide, strongly alkaline. RaSO₄: the least soluble sulfate. (Trends continue down the group.)

practice.q: A white solid is either MgCO₃ or BaCO₃. Suggest a heating test to tell them apart.
practice.a: Heat both with a Bunsen and pass the gas into limewater: MgCO₃ decomposes easily (limewater turns milky quickly); BaCO₃ barely decomposes at Bunsen temperatures.

practice.q: Explain why Ca(OH)₂ is used on fields but must not be over-applied.
practice.a: It neutralises acids in the soil (raises pH). Being slightly soluble and a strong base, too much makes the soil too alkaline for crops.

assessment.q: Which Group 2 metal reacts most vigorously with water?
Which hydroxide is the most soluble?
assessment.why: Hydroxide solubility increases down the group.

assessment.q: Which sulfate is the least soluble?
assessment.why: Sulfate solubility decreases down the group.

assessment.q: Which carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature?
Mg is heated in steam. The products are…
What volume of CO₂ (room conditions) forms from 0.10 mol of CaCO₃ heated strongly?

Ba has a full d sub-shell
assessment.why: Distance and shielding win over nuclear charge.

assessment.q: A solution gives a white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. It contains…
assessment.why: BaSO₄ is insoluble even in acid.

assessment_s.q:
This question is about calcium and its compounds.
(a) Write an equation for the reaction of calcium with water and describe two observations. [3]
(b) The solution is filtered and CO₂ is bubbled through it. State and explain what is seen. [2]
(c) Calcium nitrate is heated strongly. Write the equation and give two observations. [3]
assessment_s.a:
(a) Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂; fizzing; cloudy/white suspension forms and the calcium disappears
(b) turns milky/cloudy: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O, insoluble CaCO₃
(c) 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂; brown gas; glowing splint relights (white solid remains)

assessment_s.q:
The thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates increases down the group.
(a) Explain this trend. [2]
(b) 2.00 g of an unknown Group 2 carbonate loses 0.879 g when heated to constant mass. Identify the carbonate. Show your working. [3]
assessment_s.a:
(a) cations get larger down the group (same 2+ charge), so their charge density falls and they polarise (distort) the carbonate ion less, so it is harder to break up
(b) mass lost = CO₂: n = 0.879/44.0 = 0.0200 mol = n(MCO₃); M = 2.00/0.0200 = 100; metal = 100 − 60 = 40 → CaCO₃

pp.skill: Explaining the increase in reactivity down Group 2
pp.mis: Linking reactivity to the number of protons alone
pp.stem: Which statement explains why barium reacts with water more vigorously than calcium?
opts: Barium has more protons, so it attracts water more strongly.
Barium atoms are larger, so their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, and are lost more easily.
Barium has a higher first ionisation energy.
Barium hydroxide is less soluble than calcium hydroxide.
pp.exp: Down the group the outer electrons are further away and better shielded, so the first and second ionisation energies fall and the atoms lose electrons (are oxidised) more easily.

pp.skill: Ionisation energy and reactivity of Mg and Ba
pp.mis: Getting the direction of one of the trends wrong
pp.stem: Which row compares magnesium and barium correctly?
opts: first IE: Mg higher; rate with dilute HCl: Mg slower
first IE: Mg higher; rate with dilute HCl: Mg faster
first IE: Mg lower; rate with dilute HCl: Mg slower
first IE: Mg lower; rate with dilute HCl: Mg faster
pp.exp: Mg’s outer electrons are closer to the nucleus and less shielded: higher IE, so Mg reacts more slowly than Ba.

pp.skill: Comparing a Group 1 and a Group 2 element in the same period
pp.mis: Thinking the Group 2 ion is larger
pp.stem: Potassium and calcium are both in Period 4. Which row is correct?
opts: larger ion: K⁺; higher melting point: Ca
larger ion: K⁺; higher melting point: K
larger ion: Ca²⁺; higher melting point: Ca
larger ion: Ca²⁺; higher melting point: K
pp.exp: K⁺ and Ca²⁺ have the same electron arrangement, but Ca²⁺ has one more proton, so it is smaller. Ca gives two delocalised electrons per atom and has smaller, doubly charged ions: stronger metallic bonding.

pp.skill: Predicting properties of radium from Group 2 trends
pp.mis: Reversing the sulfate or hydroxide trend
pp.stem: Radium is below barium in Group 2. Which prediction is correct?
opts: Radium has the highest first ionisation energy in Group 2.
Radium hydroxide is the least soluble Group 2 hydroxide.
Radium sulfate is the least soluble Group 2 sulfate.
Radium carbonate has the lowest thermal stability in Group 2.
pp.exp: Down the group: sulfates become less soluble, hydroxides more soluble, carbonates more thermally stable and ionisation energies lower. Radium continues all these trends.

pp.skill: A property that decreases from Mg to Ba
pp.mis: Mixing up the hydroxide and sulfate solubility trends
pp.stem: Which property decreases from magnesium to barium?
opts: reactivity of the metals with water
pp.exp: MgSO₄ is soluble; BaSO₄ is very insoluble. The other three increase down the group.

pp.skill: Comparing calcium and magnesium compounds
pp.mis: Reversing a trend
pp.stem: Compare calcium with magnesium. In which pair is the calcium compound or element placed correctly?
opts: lower decomposition temperature of carbonate: CaCO₃
pp.exp: Hydroxide solubility increases down the group. Sulfate solubility decreases; thermal stability increases; reducing power increases (electrons lost more easily).

pp.skill: Comparing calcium and strontium and their compounds
pp.mis: Thinking heavier carbonates give more CO₂ per mole
pp.stem: Which statement comparing calcium and strontium, or their compounds, is correct?
opts: Calcium reacts with water more rapidly than strontium.
One mole of CaCO₃ gives the same amount of CO₂ with excess HCl as one mole of SrCO₃.
Calcium sulfate is less soluble in water than strontium sulfate.
Calcium hydroxide is more soluble in water than strontium hydroxide.
pp.exp: MCO₃ + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂: one mole of CO₂ per mole of carbonate either way. The other statements reverse the trends.

pp.skill: Properties of a Group 2 hydroxide
pp.mis: Thinking calcium hydroxide is very soluble
pp.stem: Calcium reacts with cold water to give compound K and hydrogen. Which is not a property of K?
opts: It is very soluble, giving a solution of pH 14.
pp.exp: K is Ca(OH)₂ (M<sub>r</sub> 74.1), a white solid that is only slightly soluble; its saturated solution (limewater) has pH about 12.

pp.skill: Reactions of Group 2 oxides and metals with water
pp.mis: Thinking oxides give hydrogen with water
pp.stem: A student writes four notes about Group 2. Which note is correct?
opts: SrO + H₂O gives Sr(OH)₂ and H₂ gas.
Heated magnesium + steam gives Mg(OH)₂ + H₂.
MgO only slightly dissolves, giving a weakly alkaline solution.
pp.exp: MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂, only slightly soluble (pH about 9). Oxides give hydroxides only, no H₂. CaO reacts vigorously (slaking). Mg with steam gives MgO + H₂.

pp.skill: Identifying a substance from its reactions with water and acid
pp.mis: Choosing an oxide when a gas is given off
pp.stem: Substance J reacts very slowly with cold water, giving a few bubbles of gas and a weakly alkaline solution. When dilute sulfuric acid is added to the solution, no precipitate forms. What is J?
pp.exp: A gas (H₂) means a metal, not an oxide. Very slow reaction and a soluble sulfate (no precipitate) → magnesium. Barium reacts fast and gives a BaSO₄ precipitate.

pp.skill: Explaining why a reaction with sulfuric acid stops
pp.mis: Blaming a lower reactivity
pp.stem: Magnesium and barium are each added to an excess of dilute sulfuric acid. Magnesium dissolves completely; barium reacts vigorously at first, then stops with most of it unreacted. Why?
opts: Barium is less reactive than magnesium.
A layer of insoluble barium sulfate forms on the barium.
Barium forms a protective oxide layer.
The acid is used up by the barium.
pp.exp: BaSO₄ is insoluble and coats the metal, stopping further reaction. MgSO₄ is soluble, so magnesium dissolves completely.

pp.skill: Identifying a solid from solution tests
pp.mis: Forgetting which sulfates are soluble
pp.stem: Solid W reacts with water to give a weakly alkaline solution. Adding dilute H₂SO₄ to this solution gives no precipitate. What could W be?
pp.exp: MgO → Mg(OH)₂ (slightly soluble, weakly alkaline); MgSO₄ is soluble, so no precipitate. BaO and SrO give insoluble sulfates; BaCO₃ does not dissolve.

pp.skill: Identifying compounds from the pH of their mixtures with water
pp.mis: Assuming every Group 2 compound is alkaline
pp.stem: Two Group 2 compounds, V and W, are each shaken with water. V gives pH 12.4; W gives pH 7. Which row could identify V and W?
pp.exp: Saturated Ca(OH)₂ has pH about 12.4. Sulfates are neutral salts. Mg(OH)₂ is so sparingly soluble that it gives only about pH 9–10.

pp.skill: Mixing two clear solutions to form a precipitate
pp.mis: Choosing an insoluble starting compound
pp.stem: Two Group 2 compounds each dissolve completely in water to give clear solutions. When the solutions are mixed, a white precipitate forms. Which pair could they be?
pp.exp: Both dissolve; Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s). BaSO₄ and Mg(OH)₂ do not dissolve in the first place; MgCl₂ + Ba(NO₃)₂ gives no precipitate.

pp.skill: Following precipitates through a sequence of reagents
pp.mis: Thinking all precipitates dissolve in acid
pp.stem: Strontium hydroxide solution is shaken with MgSO₄(aq), giving a white precipitate. An excess of dilute HCl is then added. What is seen?
opts: all the precipitate dissolves to give a clear solution
pp.exp: The precipitate contains Mg(OH)₂ and SrSO₄. HCl dissolves the Mg(OH)₂, but SrSO₄ is insoluble in acid, so some white solid remains.

pp.skill: Separating and testing products of a reaction mixture
pp.mis: Mixing up which product is in solution
pp.stem: Strontium oxide and magnesium chloride are stirred into water and filtered, giving solution Y and white solid Z. Y and Z are each added to an excess of dilute H₂SO₄. What is seen?
opts: Y: white precipitate; Z: dissolves to a colourless solution
Y: colourless solution; Z: white precipitate
Y: colourless solution; Z: colourless solution
Y: white precipitate; Z: no change
pp.exp: SrO + H₂O → Sr(OH)₂; with MgCl₂, Mg(OH)₂ precipitates (Z) and Sr²⁺ stays in solution (Y). Y + H₂SO₄ → SrSO₄ precipitate. Z (a base) dissolves in acid to give MgSO₄(aq).

pp.skill: Identifying an anion with a Group 2 salt and acid
pp.mis: Confusing sulfate and carbonate tests
pp.stem: Solution R gives a white precipitate with Ba(NO₃)₂(aq). When dilute HNO₃ is added to R, bubbles of a colourless gas appear. Which anion is in R?
pp.exp: Carbonate gives BaCO₃ (white) and fizzes with acid (CO₂). Sulfate gives BaSO₄ but no gas with acid.

pp.skill: Agricultural uses of calcium compounds
pp.mis: Thinking CaCO₃ is more soluble than Ca(OH)₂
pp.stem:
Slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂, and powdered limestone, CaCO₃, are both used on acidic soil.
1 Both raise the pH of the soil.
2 One mole of each neutralises the same amount of H⁺ ions.
3 Ca(OH)₂ is less soluble in water than CaCO₃.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: Each neutralises 2 mol H⁺ per mole (Ca(OH)₂ + 2H⁺; CaCO₃ + 2H⁺). Ca(OH)₂ is slightly soluble and acts faster; CaCO₃ is much less soluble.

pp.skill: Two trends down Group 2
pp.mis: Assuming all properties change the same way
pp.stem: How do the thermal stability of the carbonates and the solubility of the hydroxides change from Mg to Ba?
pp.exp: Both increase down the group. (Sulfate solubility is the one that decreases.)

pp.skill: Comparing solubility and stability for two elements
pp.mis: Reversing one trend
pp.stem: Which row is correct for compounds of calcium and strontium?
opts: less soluble sulfate: SrSO₄; less stable nitrate: Ca(NO₃)₂
less soluble sulfate: CaSO₄; less stable nitrate: Ca(NO₃)₂
less soluble sulfate: SrSO₄; less stable nitrate: Sr(NO₃)₂
less soluble sulfate: CaSO₄; less stable nitrate: Sr(NO₃)₂
pp.exp: Sulfates are less soluble lower down (Sr). Nitrates are less stable higher up (Ca decomposes at a lower temperature).

pp.skill: Using one trend to predict others for an unknown element
pp.mis: Not working out where X is in the group
pp.stem: CaCO₃ decomposes at 840 °C. For Group 2 element X, the carbonate decomposes at 1280 °C. Compared with calcium, what are the solubilities of the sulfate and hydroxide of X?
opts: sulfate less soluble; hydroxide more soluble
sulfate more soluble; hydroxide less soluble
pp.exp: A more stable carbonate means X is below Ca (Sr or Ba). Lower down: sulfates less soluble, hydroxides more soluble.

pp.skill: Identifying Group 2 elements from combined clues
pp.mis: Not using every clue
pp.stem: W, X, Y and Z are Mg, Ca, Sr and Ba in some order. W has the least soluble hydroxide. X has the least soluble sulfate. Y reacts with water faster than Z. What is Y?
pp.exp: Least soluble hydroxide → W = Mg. Least soluble sulfate → X = Ba. Y and Z are Ca and Sr; the faster one, Y, is strontium.

pp.skill: Following a two-step sequence for a Group 2 element
pp.mis: Stopping at the first product
pp.stem: Element Q is Mg or Sr. Q’s carbonate decomposes at a lower temperature than CaCO₃. Q is heated in oxygen, then the product is added to water. What is the final product?
pp.exp: Less stable carbonate than CaCO₃ → above Ca → Mg. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂.

pp.skill: Identity and thermal decomposition equation
pp.mis: Writing the metal as a product
pp.stem: X is a Group 2 element in Period 4 or 6. X(OH)₂ is more soluble than Sr(OH)₂. Which row is correct?
opts: X is Ca; XCO₃ → X + CO₂ + ½O₂
X is Ca; XCO₃ → XO + CO₂
X is Ba; XCO₃ → X + CO₂ + ½O₂
X is Ba; XCO₃ → XO + CO₂
pp.exp: More soluble hydroxide than Sr(OH)₂ → below Sr → Ba (Period 6). Carbonates decompose to the oxide and CO₂.

pp.skill: Writing the decomposition of a Group 2 carbonate
pp.mis: Producing the metal or the wrong oxide formula
pp.stem: Radium is below barium in Group 2. Which equation shows what happens when radium carbonate is heated very strongly?
pp.exp: Group 2 carbonates decompose to the oxide MO and CO₂. (Radium’s carbonate needs a very high temperature, as stability increases down the group.)

pp.skill: Correct equation for a nitrate decomposition
pp.mis: Choosing NO instead of NO₂
pp.stem: Which equation for the thermal decomposition of strontium nitrate is correct?
pp.exp: Group 2 nitrates give the oxide, brown NO₂ and O₂ in the ratio 2 : 4 : 1.

pp.skill: Gases from heating a hydrated nitrate
pp.mis: Thinking hydrogen is released
pp.stem: Hydrated calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂·4H₂O, is heated strongly. Which three gases are given off?
opts: water vapour, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen
water vapour, nitrogen monoxide and oxygen
pp.exp: First the water of crystallisation is driven off, then 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂.

pp.skill: Comparing nitrate decompositions with an indicator
pp.mis: Expecting an alkaline gas
pp.stem: Mg(NO₃)₂ and Ba(NO₃)₂ are heated in identical tubes. The gases bubble through water containing universal indicator. Which describes the colour change and which nitrate changes it first?
pp.exp: NO₂ dissolves to form an acidic solution (red). Mg(NO₃)₂ is less thermally stable, so it decomposes sooner.

pp.skill: A decomposition gas that is a pollutant
pp.mis: Thinking CO₂ causes smog
pp.stem: Which compound, on heating, releases a gas that contributes to both acid rain and photochemical smog?
pp.exp: Nitrates release NO₂, which forms HNO₃ in rain and reacts with hydrocarbons to form PAN in smog.

pp.skill: Moles of gas from a nitrate decomposition
pp.mis: Counting only NO₂
pp.stem: 2.0 mol of anhydrous strontium nitrate is completely decomposed by heating. What is the total amount of gas produced?
pp.exp: 2Sr(NO₃)₂ → 2SrO + 4NO₂ + O₂: 2 mol of nitrate gives 4 + 1 = 5 mol of gas.

pp.skill: Volume of gas from a nitrate decomposition
pp.mis: Forgetting the oxygen
pp.stem: What total volume of gas, measured at room conditions, is produced when 0.020 mol of anhydrous calcium nitrate is completely decomposed?
pp.exp: Each mole of Ca(NO₃)₂ gives 2 mol NO₂ + ½ mol O₂ = 2.5 mol gas. 0.020 × 2.5 = 0.050 mol × 24 000 = 1200 cm³.

pp.skill: Volume of oxygen from a nitrate
pp.mis: Using a 1 : 1 ratio for oxygen
pp.stem: What volume of oxygen, at room conditions, is produced when 0.80 mol of magnesium nitrate decomposes completely?

pp.skill: Volumes of each gas from a nitrate
pp.mis: Mixing up the two gas ratios
pp.stem: Calcium nitrate (0.050 mol, anhydrous) is heated to constant mass. Find the volume of each gas evolved (room conditions).

pp.skill: Mass of oxygen from a nitrate decomposition
pp.mis: Using the nitrate:O₂ ratio as 1 : 1
pp.stem: 32.8 g of anhydrous calcium nitrate (M<sub>r</sub> 164.1) is heated until no further change. What mass of oxygen is produced?

pp.skill: Identifying a nitrate from the mass of gas released
pp.mis: Forgetting that both NO₂ and O₂ leave
pp.stem: 4.00 g of an anhydrous Group 2 nitrate is heated until there is no further change. The mass falls by 2.63 g. Which nitrate was it?
pp.exp: Per mole of nitrate, 2 mol NO₂ + ½ mol O₂ leave = 92 + 16 = 108 g. n = 2.63/108 = 0.0244 mol, so M = 4.00/0.0244 = 164: Ca(NO₃)₂.

pp.skill: Greatest volume of gas from equal masses
pp.mis: Comparing only the formula masses
pp.stem: 1.0 g samples of MgCO₃, Mg(NO₃)₂, BaCO₃ and Ba(NO₃)₂ are each decomposed to the oxide. Which gives the greatest volume of gas?
pp.exp: Moles of gas per gram: MgCO₃ 1/84.3 = 0.0119; Mg(NO₃)₂ 2.5/148.3 = 0.0169; BaCO₃ 0.0051; Ba(NO₃)₂ 0.0096.

pp.skill: Smallest volume of gas from equal masses
pp.mis: Assuming carbonates always give least
pp.stem: Equal masses of CaCO₃, Ca(NO₃)₂, SrCO₃ and Sr(NO₃)₂ are fully decomposed. Which gives the smallest volume of gas?
pp.exp: Moles of gas per gram: CaCO₃ 0.0100; Ca(NO₃)₂ 0.0152; SrCO₃ 1/147.6 = 0.0068; Sr(NO₃)₂ 0.0118.

pp.skill: Two trends down the carbonates
pp.mis: Linking higher stability with more gas
pp.stem: Going down Group 2, how do the thermal stability of the carbonates and the volume of CO₂ from fully decomposing 1.0 g of carbonate change?
pp.exp: Stability increases down the group. Molar mass increases, so 1.0 g contains fewer moles and gives less CO₂.

pp.skill: Counting the products of decomposing a mixture
pp.mis: Counting the same gas twice
pp.stem: A mixture of CaCO₃ and SrCO₃ is heated strongly until both decompose completely. How many different products form?
pp.exp: CaO, SrO and CO₂ (from both): three different substances.

pp.skill: Comparing moles of gas from different reactions
pp.mis: Not converting each mass to moles
pp.stem: Which produces the smallest amount of gas? [M: Mg 24.3; CaCO₃ 100.1; Sr(NO₃)₂ 211.6; BaCO₃ 197.3]
opts: 4.86 g Mg with an excess of dilute HCl
10.0 g CaCO₃ with an excess of dilute HCl

pp.skill: Ionisation energy trend, reaction with water and thermal decomposition
pp.stem: The Group 2 elements Mg to Ba show trends in their properties.

parts.q: The sum of the first two ionisation energies falls from Mg to Ba. Explain this trend.
ms: outer electrons are further from the nucleus (more shells) and more shielded
so less energy is needed to remove them, despite the greater nuclear charge

parts.q: Write an equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of barium with water.
Samples of the solution are tested with dilute HCl and with dilute H₂SO₄. State what you would see in each.

parts.q: Describe what is seen when solid magnesium nitrate is heated strongly.
ms: white solid melts/decomposes, leaving a white solid (MgO)
brown gas (NO₂) given off (and a gas that relights a glowing splint)
